entries.c2bc72d7267aa42f69257b9a0c499dedb0f98b2a: <div sID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="137" osisID="Ps.137" sID="Ps.137"/> <div eID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13109" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13110" type="x-p"/> There are divers psalms which are thought to have been penned in the latter days of the Jewish church, when prophecy was near expiring and the canon of the Old Testament ready to be closed up, but none of them appears so plainly to be of a late date as this, which was penned when the people of God were captives in Babylon, and there insulted over by these proud oppressors; probably it was towards the latter end of their captivity; for now they saw the destruction of Babylon hastening on apace (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">ver. 8</reference>), which would be their discharge. It is a mournful psalm, a lamentation; and the Septuagint makes it one of the lamentations of Jeremiah, naming him for the author of it. Here I. The melancholy captives cannot enjoy themselves, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. They cannot humour their proud oppressors, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.3-Ps.137.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. They cannot forget Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.5-Ps.137.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. IV. They cannot forgive Edom and Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7-Ps.137.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. In singing this psalm we must be much affected with the concernments of the church, especially that part of it that is in affliction, laying the sorrows of God's people near our hearts, comforting ourselves in the prospect of the deliverance of the church and the ruin of its enemies, in due time, but carefully avoiding all personal animosities, and not mixing the leaven of malice with our sacrifices.
entries.68e90a4094c0363b610e8bfaa5d3384b4aebce20: <div eID="gen13110" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13109" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sorrows of Captivity.</title> <div sID="gen13111" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. <hi type="super">2</hi> We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. <hi type="super">3</hi> For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us <hi type="italic">required of us</hi> mirth, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Sing us <hi type="italic">one</hi> of the songs of Zion. <hi type="super">4</hi> How shall we sing the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's song in a strange land? <hi type="super">5</hi> If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget <hi type="italic">her cunning.</hi> <hi type="super">6</hi> If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy. <div eID="gen13111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13112" type="x-p"/> We have here the daughter of Zion covered with a cloud, and dwelling with the daughter of Babylon; the people of God in tears, but sowing in tears. Observe, <div eID="gen13112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13113" type="x-p"/> I. The mournful posture they were in as to their affairs and as to their spirits. 1. They were posted <hi type="italic">by the rivers of Babylon,</hi> in a strange land, a great way from their own country, whence they were brought as prisoners of war. The land of Babylon was now a house of bondage to that people, as Egypt had been in their beginning. Their conquerors quartered them <hi type="italic">by the rivers,</hi> with design to employ them there, and keep them to work in their galleys; or perhaps they chose it as the most melancholy place, and therefore most suitable to their sorrowful spirits. If they must build houses there (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.5">Jer. xxix. 5</reference>), it shall not be in the cities, the places of concourse, but by the rivers, the places of solitude, where they might mingle their tears with the streams. We find some of them by the <hi type="italic">river Chebar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.3">Ezek. i. 3</reference>), others by the <hi type="italic">river Ulai,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.8.2">Dan. viii. 2</reference>. 2. There they <hi type="italic">sat down</hi> to indulge their grief by poring on their miseries. Jeremiah had taught them under this yoke to <hi type="italic">sit alone,</hi> and <hi type="italic">keep silence,</hi> and <hi type="italic">put their mouths in the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.28-Lam.3.29">Lam. iii. 28, 29</reference>. "We sat down, as those that expected to stay, and were content, since it was the will of God that it must be so." 3. Thoughts of Zion drew tears from their eyes; and it was not a sudden passion of weeping, such as we are sometimes put into by a trouble that surprises us, but they were deliberate tears (we <hi type="italic">sat down and wept</hi>), tears with consideration—we <hi type="italic">wept when we remembered Zion,</hi> the holy hill on which the temple was built. Their affection to God's house swallowed up their concern for their own houses. They remembered Zion's former glory and the satisfaction they had had in Zion's courts, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.7">Lam. i. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Jerusalem remembered, in the days of her misery, all her pleasant things which she had in the days of old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Ps. xlii. 4</reference>. They remembered Zion's present desolations, and <hi type="italic">favoured the dust thereof,</hi> which was a good sign that the time for God to favour it was not far off, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.14">Ps. cii. 13, 14</reference>. 4. They laid by their instruments of music (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">We hung our harps upon the willows.</hi> (1.) The harps they used for their own diversion and entertainment. These they laid aside, both because it was their judgment that they ought not to use them now that God called to weeping and mourning (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.12">Isa. xxii. 12</reference>), and their spirits were so sad that they had no hearts to use them; they brought their harps with them, designing perhaps to use them for the alleviating of their grief, but it proved so great that it would not admit the experiment. Music makes some people melancholy. <hi type="italic">As vinegar upon nitre, so is he that sings songs to a heavy heart.</hi> (2.) The harps they used in God's worship, the Levites' harps. These they did not throw away, hoping they might yet again have occasion to use them, but they laid them aside because they had no present use for them; God had cut them out other work by <hi type="italic">turning their feasting into mourning and their songs into lamentations,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.8.10">Amos viii. 10</reference>. Every thing is beautiful in its season. They did not hide their harps in the bushes, or the hollows of the rocks; but hung them up in view, that the sight of them might affect them with this deplorable change. Yet perhaps they were faulty in doing this; for praising God is never out of season; it is his will that we should <hi type="italic">in every thing give thanks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.24.15-Isa.24.16">Isa. xxiv. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen13113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13114" type="x-p"/> II. The abuses which their enemies put upon them when they were in this melancholy condition, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">v. 3</reference>. They had <hi type="italic">carried them away captive</hi> from their own land and then <hi type="italic">wasted them</hi> in the land of their captivity, took what little they had from them. But this was not enough; to complete their woes they insulted over them: They <hi type="italic">required of us mirth and a song.</hi> Now, 1. This was very barbarous and inhuman; even an enemy, in misery, is to be pitied and not trampled upon. It argues a base and sordid spirit to upbraid those that are in distress either with their former joys or with their present griefs, or to challenge those to be merry who, we know, are out of tune for it. This is adding affliction to the afflicted. 2. It was very profane and impious. No songs would serve them but the <hi type="italic">songs of Zion,</hi> with which God had been honoured; so that in this demand they reflected upon God himself as Belshazzar, when he drank wine in temple-bowls. Their enemies <hi type="italic">mocked at their sabbaths,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.1.7">Lam. i. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen13114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13115" type="x-p"/> III. The patience wherewith they bore these abuses, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.4">v. 4</reference>. They had laid by their harps, and would not resume them, no, not to ingratiate themselves with those at whose mercy they lay; they would not answer those fools according to their folly. Profane scoffers are not to be humoured, nor pearls cast before swine. David prudently <hi type="italic">kept silence even from good</hi> when the <hi type="italic">wicked were before him,</hi> who, he knew, would ridicule what he said and make a jest of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.2">Ps. xxxix. 1, 2</reference>. The reason they gave is very mild and pious: <hi type="italic">How shall we sing the Lord's song in a strange land?</hi> They do not say, "How shall we sing when we are so much in sorrow?" If that had been all, they might perhaps have put a force upon themselves so far as to oblige their masters with a song; but "It is the <hi type="italic">Lord's song;</hi> it is a sacred thing; it is peculiar to the temple-service, and therefore we dare not sing it in the land of a stranger, among idolaters." We must not serve common mirth, much less profane mirth, with any thing that is appropriated to God, who is sometimes to be honoured by a religious silence as well as by religious speaking. <div eID="gen13115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13116" type="x-p"/> IV. The constant affection they retained for Jerusalem, the city of their solemnities, even now that they were in Babylon. Though their enemies banter them for talking so much of Jerusalem, and even doting upon it, their love to it is not in the least abated; it is what they may be jeered for, but will never be jeered out of, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.5-Ps.137.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen13116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13117" type="x-p"/> 1. How these pious captives stood affected to Jerusalem. (1.) Their heads were full of it. It was always in their minds; they remembered it; they did not forget it, though they had been long absent from it; many of them had never seen it, nor knew any thing of it but by report, and by what they had read in the scripture, yet it was graven upon the palms of their hands, and even its ruins were continually before them, which was an evidence of their faith in the promise of its restoration in due time. In their daily prayers they opened their windows towards Jerusalem; and how then could they forget it? (2.) Their hearts were full of it. They <hi type="italic">preferred</hi> it <hi type="italic">above</hi> their <hi type="italic">chief joy,</hi> and therefore they remembered it and could not forget it. What we love we love to think of. Those that rejoice in God do, for his sake, make Jerusalem their joy, and prefer it before that, whatever it is, which is the head of their joy, which is dearest to them in this world. A godly man will prefer a public good before any private satisfaction or gratification whatsoever. <div eID="gen13117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13118" type="x-p"/> 2. How stedfastly they resolved to keep up this affection, which they express by a solemn imprecation of mischief to themselves if they should let it fall: "Let me be for ever disabled either to sing or play on the harp if I so far forget the religion of my country as to make use of my songs and harps for the pleasing of Babylon's sons or the praising of Babylon's gods. <hi type="italic">Let my right hand forget her art</hi>" (which the hand of an expert musician never can, unless it be withered), "nay, <hi type="italic">let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth,</hi> if I have not a good word to say for Jerusalem wherever I am." Though they dare not sing Zion's songs among the Babylonians, yet they cannot forget them, but, as soon as ever the present restraint is taken off, they will sing them as readily as ever, notwithstanding the long disuse.
entries.e5e445bfbe0528a30b6c7b6342cc44d6426cf8f6: <div eID="gen13118" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sorrows of Captivity.</title> <div sID="gen13119" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Remember, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase <hi type="italic">it,</hi> rase <hi type="italic">it, even</hi> to the foundation thereof. <hi type="super">8</hi> O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy <hi type="italic">shall he be,</hi> that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us. <hi type="super">9</hi> Happy <hi type="italic">shall he be,</hi> that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones. <div eID="gen13119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13120" type="x-p"/> The pious Jews in Babylon, having afflicted themselves with the thoughts of the ruins of Jerusalem, here please themselves with the prospect of the ruin of her impenitent implacable enemies; but this not from a spirit of revenge, but from a holy zeal for the glory of God and the honour of his kingdom. <div eID="gen13120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13121" type="x-p"/> I. The Edomites will certainly be reckoned with, and all others that were accessaries to the destruction of Jerusalem, that were aiding and abetting, that <hi type="italic">helped forward the affliction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.15">Zech. i. 15</reference>) and triumphed in it, that <hi type="italic">said, in the day of Jerusalem,</hi> the day of her judgment, "<hi type="italic">Rase it, rase it to the foundations;</hi> down with it, down with it; do not leave one stone upon another." Thus they made the Chaldean army more furious, who were already so enraged that they needed no spur. Thus they put shame upon Israel, who would be looked upon as a people worthy to be cut off when their next neighbours had such an ill-will to them. And all this was a fruit of the old enmity of Esau against Jacob, because he got the birthright and the blessing, and a branch of that more ancient enmity between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent: <hi type="italic">Lord, remember</hi> them, says the psalmist, which is an appeal to his justice against them. Far be it from us to avenge ourselves, if ever it should be in our power, but we will leave it to him who has said, <hi type="italic">Vengeance is mine.</hi> Note, Those that are glad at calamities, especially the calamities of Jerusalem, shall not go unpunished. Those that are confederate with the persecutors of good people, and stir them up, and set them on, and are pleased with what they do, shall certainly be called to an account for it against another day, and God will remember it against them. <div eID="gen13121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13122" type="x-p"/> II. Babylon is the principal, and it will come to her turn too to drink of the cup of tremblings, the very dregs of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.8-Ps.137.9">v. 8, 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">O daughter of Babylon!</hi> proud and secure as thou art, we know well, by the scriptures of truth, thou <hi type="italic">art to be destroyed,</hi> or (as Dr. Hammond reads it) <hi type="italic">who art the destroyer.</hi> The destroyers shall be destroyed, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>. And perhaps it is with reference to this that the man of sin, the head of the New-Testament Babylon, is called a <hi type="italic">son of perdition,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2 Thess. ii. 3</reference>. The destruction of Babylon being foreseen as a sure destruction (thou <hi type="italic">art to be destroyed</hi>), it is spoken of, 1. As a just destruction. She shall be paid in her own coin: "Thou shalt be served <hi type="italic">as thou hast served us,</hi> as barbarously used by the destroyers as we have been by thee," See <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Rev. xviii. 6</reference>. Let not those expect to find mercy who, when they had power, did not show mercy. 2. As an utter destruction. The very little ones of Babylon, when it is taken by storm, and all in it are put to the sword, shall be dashed to pieces by the enraged and merciless conqueror. None escape if these little ones perish. Those are the seed of another generation; so that, if they be cut off, the ruin will be not only total, as Jerusalem's was, but final. It is sunk like a millstone into the sea, never to rise. 3. As a destruction which should reflect honour upon the instruments of it. Happy shall those be that do it; for they are fulfilling God's counsels; and therefore he calls Cyrus, who did it, his <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> his <hi type="italic">shepherd,</hi> his <hi type="italic">anointed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa. xliv. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">xlv. 1</reference>), and the soldiers that were employed in it his <hi type="italic">sanctified ones,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.13.3">Isa. xiii. 3</reference>. They are making way for the enlargement of God's Israel, and happy are those who are in any way serviceable to that. The fall of the New-Testament Babylon will be the triumph of all the saints, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.1">Rev. xix. 1</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.137"/> <div eID="gen13122" type="x-p"/>

entries.0aafde2f0e7bc6770f7a945ded66a4d22b4cfd92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7072"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 137</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9">Psa 137:1-9</reference>. This Psalm records the mourning of the captive Israelites, and a prayer and prediction respecting the destruction of their enemies.</title> <div sID="gen10846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7072"/><hi type="bold">1. rivers of Babylon--</hi>the name of the city used for the whole country.<div eID="gen10846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remembered Zion--</hi>or, Jerusalem, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.132.13">Psa 132:13</reference>. <div eID="gen10847" type="x-p"/>
entries.03128a862776cdf67bb41fce6ba78d176fce8b9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7073"/><div sID="gen10848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7073"/><hi type="bold">2. upon the willows--</hi>which may have grown there then, if not now; as the palm, which was once common, is now rare in Palestine. <div eID="gen10848" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ec9cff08e17b9a6c6a2f9026a2e7f6171eaef7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7074"/><div sID="gen10849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7074"/>3-4. Whether the request was in curiosity or derision, the answer intimates that a compliance was incongruous with their mournful feelings (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.20">Pr 25:20</reference>). <div eID="gen10849" type="x-p"/>
entries.381e8b747d21259e83f19e6659a223689bb739f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7075"/><div sID="gen10850" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7075"/>5-6. For joyful songs would imply forgetfulness of their desolated homes and fallen Church. The solemn imprecations on the hand and tongue, if thus forgetful, relate to the cunning or skill in playing, and the power of singing. <div eID="gen10850" type="x-p"/>
entries.a96452dafe23945bdfb76a50d5042210752e645e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7076"/><div sID="gen10851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7076"/><hi type="bold">7-9. Remember ... the children of Edom--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.132.1">Psa 132:1</reference>), that is, to punish.<div eID="gen10851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the day of Jerusalem--</hi>its downfall (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">22</reference>; Ob 11-13). <div eID="gen10852" type="x-p"/>

entries.60f6bb9788cc4d21c6560b8094a600a227c382ac: <div eID="gen23267" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23268" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23269" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23269" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23268" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23270" type="x-p"/> The desolate and afflicted state of the captives in Babylon, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.1">Psa 137:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.2">Psa 137:2</reference>. How they were insulted by their enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.3">Psa 137:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.4">Psa 137:4</reference>. Their attachment to their country, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.5">Psa 137:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.6">Psa 137:6</reference>. Judgments denounced against their enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.7-Psa.137.9">Psa 137:7-9</reference>. <div eID="gen23270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23271" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, say, ridiculously enough, a Psalm of David for Jeremiah. Anachronisms with those who wrote the titles to the Psalms were matters of no importance. Jeremiah never was at Babylon; and therefore could have no part in a Psalm that was sung on the banks of its rivers by the Israelitish captives. Neither the Hebrew nor Chaldee has any title; the Syriac attributes it to David. Some think it was sung when they returned from Babylon; others, while they were there. It is a matter of little importance. It was evidently composed during or at the close of the captivity. <div eID="gen23271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23272" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23273" type="x-p"/> By the rivers of Babylon - These might have been the Tigris and Euphrates, or their branches, or streams that flowed into them. In their captivity and dispersion, it was customary for the Jews to hold their religious meetings on the banks of rivers. Mention is made of this <reference osisRef="Act.16.13">Act 16:13</reference>, where we find the Jews of Philippi resorting to a river side, where prayer was wont to be made. And sometimes they built their synagogues here, when they were expelled from the cities.
entries.b1c9b359e31b511c6575f8a01a7141233c7ca336: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23274" type="x-p"/> We hanged our harps upon the willows - The ערבים arabim or willows were very plentiful in Babylon. The great quantity of them that were on the banks of the Euphrates caused Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.7">Isa 15:7</reference>, to call it the brook or river of willows. This is a most affecting picture. Perhaps resting themselves after toil, and wishing to spend their time religiously, they took their harps, and were about to sing one of the songs of Zion; but, reflecting on their own country, they became so filled with distress, that they unstrung their harps with one consent, and hung them on the willow bushes, and gave a general loose to their grief. Some of the Babylonians, who probably attended such meetings for the sake of the music, being present at the time here specified, desired them to sing one of Zion's songs: this is affectingly told.
entries.2af938acf83040fec79409431d6e92e81610506c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23275" type="x-p"/> They that carried us away captive required of us a song - This was as unreasonable as it was insulting. How could they who had reduced us to slavery, and dragged us in chains from our own beautiful land and privileges, expect us to sing a sacred ode to please them, who were enemies both to us and to our God? And how could those who wasted us expect mirth from people in captivity, deprived of all their possessions, and in the most abject state of poverty and oppression?
entries.b3c89fd4baee98db90bf982ed5bf933b2ba671c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23276" type="x-p"/> How shall we sing the Lord's song - איך נשיר eich! nashir; O, we sing! Who does not hear the deep sigh in the strongly guttural sound of the original איך eich! wrung, as it were, from the bottom of the heart? Can We, in this state of slavery, - We, exiles, from our country, We, stripped of all our property, - We, reduced to contempt by our strong enemy, - We, deprived of our religious privileges, - We, insulted by our oppressors, - We, in the land of heathens, - We sing, or be mirthful in these circumstances? No: God does not expect it; man should not wish it; and it is base in our enemies to require it.
entries.93eee219b2d1e2ec141a9a71da42ba04ca643535: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23277" type="x-p"/> If I forget thee, O Jerusalem - Such conduct would be, in effect, a renunciation of our land a tacit acknowledgment that we were reconciled to our bondage; a concession that we were pleased with our captivity, and could profane holy ordinances by using them as means of sport or pastime to the heathen. No: Jerusalem! we remember thee and thy Divine ordinances: and especially thy King and our God, whose indignation we must bear, because we have sinned against him. <div eID="gen23277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23278" type="x-p"/> Let my right hand forget - Let me forget the use of my right hand. Let me forget that which is dearest and most profitable to me; and let me lose my skill in the management of my harp, if I ever prostitute it to please the ungodly multitude or the enemies of my Creator!
entries.a661b16cfc723f2c969bd5b51654f40f287d1a25: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23279" type="x-p"/> Let my tongue cleave - Let me lose my voice, and all its powers of melody; my tongue, and all its faculty of speech; my ear, and its discernment of sounds; if I do not prefer my country, my people, and the ordinances of my God, beyond all these, and whatever may constitute the chiefest joy I can possess in aught else beside. This is truly patriotic, truly noble and dignified. Such sentiments can only be found in the hearts and mouths of those slaves whom the grace of God has made free.
entries.597d6737dd8b744ad12372f38b46343beee3fc67: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23280" type="x-p"/> Remember - the children of Edom - It appears from <reference osisRef="Jer.12.6">Jer 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">Jer 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">Lam 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">Lam 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.25.12">Eze 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Oba.1.11-Oba.1.14">Oba 1:11-14</reference>; that the Idumeans joined the army of Nebuchadnezzar against their brethren the Jews; and that they were main instruments in rasing the walls of Jerusalem even to the ground.
entries.72b89a90385a08894886cb938bad6c5d8fc2f0f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23281" type="x-p"/> O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed - Or, O thou daughter of Babylon the destroyer, or, who art to be ruined. In being reduced under the empire of the Persians, Babylon was already greatly humbled and brought low from what it was in the days of Nebuchadnezzar; but it was afterwards so totally ruined that not a vestige of it remains. After its capture by Cyrus, A.M. 3468, it could never be considered a capital city; but it appeared to follow the fortunes of its various conquerors till it was, as a city, finally destroyed. <div eID="gen23281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23282" type="x-p"/> Rewardeth thee as thou hast served us - This was Cyrus, who was chosen of God to do this work, and is therefore called happy, as being God's agent in its destruction. Greater desolations were afterwards brought upon it by Darius Hystaspes, who took this city after it had revolted, and slaughtered the inhabitants, men and women, in a barbarous manner. Herod. lib. iii.
entries.806e43186a7e4a1a7ae2567c4c68e97b2b03c3fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23283" type="x-p"/> Happy - that taketh and dasheth thy little ones - That is, So oppressive hast thou been to all under thy domination, as to become universally hated and detested; so that those who may have the last hand in thy destruction, and the total extermination of thy inhabitants, shall be reputed happy - shall be celebrated and extolled as those who have rid the world of a curse so grievous. These prophetic declarations contain no excitement to any person or persons to commit acts of cruelty and barbarity; but are simply declarative of what would take place in the order of the retributive providence and justice of God, and the general opinion that should in consequence be expressed on the subject; therefore praying for the destruction of our enemies is totally out of the question. It should not be omitted that the Chaldee considers this Psalm a dialogue, which it thus divides: - The three first verses are supposed to have been spoken by the psalmist, By the rivers, etc. The Levites answer from the porch of the temple, in <reference osisRef="Psa.137.4">Psa 137:4</reference>, How shall we sing, etc. The voice of the Holy Spirit responds in <reference osisRef="Psa.137.5">Psa 137:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.6">Psa 137:6</reference>, If I forget thee, etc. Michael, the prince of Jerusalem, answers in <reference osisRef="Psa.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>, Remember, O Lord, etc. Gabriel, the prince of Zion, then addresses the destroyer of the Babylonish nation, in <reference osisRef="Psa.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.137.9">Psa 137:9</reference>, Happy shall be he that rewardeth thee, etc. To slay all when a city was sacked, both male and female, old and young, was a common practice in ancient times. Homer describes this in words almost similar to those of the psalmist: - Υἱας τ' ολλυμενους, ἑλκυσθεισας τε θυγατρας, Και θαλαμους κεραΐζομενους, και νηπια τεκνα Βαλλομενα προτι γαιῃ εν αινῃ δηΐοτητι, Ἑλκομενας τε νυους ολοης ὑπο χερσιν Αχαιων. <div eID="gen23283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23284" type="x-p"/> Il. lib. xxii., ver. 62. <div eID="gen23284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23285" type="x-p"/> My heroes slain, my bridal bed o'erturned; <div eID="gen23285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23286" type="x-p"/> My daughters ravished, and my city burned: <div eID="gen23286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23287" type="x-p"/> My bleeding infants dashed against the floor; <div eID="gen23287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23288" type="x-p"/> These I have yet to see; perhaps yet more. <div eID="gen23288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23289" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen23289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23290" type="x-p"/> These excesses were common in all barbarous nations, and are only prophetically declared here. He shall be reputed happy, prosperous, and highly commendable, who shall destroy Babylon.  <chapter eID="Ps.137"/> <div eID="gen23290" type="x-p"/>

entries.0586eee1fe65f559244b0c0fe8f18700d0ac30e8: <div eID="gen10257" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">By the Rivers of Babylon</title> <div sID="gen10258" type="x-p"/> The Hallelujah Ps 135 and the Hodu Ps 136 are followed by a Psalm which glances back into the time of the Exile, when such cheerful songs as they once sang to the accompaniment of the music of the Levites at the worship of God on Mount Zion were obliged to be silent. It is anonymous. The inscription Τῷ Δαυίδ (διὰ) Ἱιερεμίου found in codices of the lxx, which is meant to say that it is a Davidic song coming from the heart of Jeremiah,<note placement="foot">Reversely Ellies du Pin (in the preface of his <hi type="italic">Bibliotèque des Auteurs Ecclésiastiques</hi>) says: <hi type="italic">Le Pseaume</hi> 136 <hi type="italic">porte le nom de David et de Jeremie, ce qu'il faut apparement entendre ainsi: Pseaume de Jeremie fait à l'imitation de David</hi>.</note> is all the more erroneous as Jeremiah never was one of the Babylonian exiles. <div eID="gen10258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10259" type="x-p"/> The שׁ, which is repeated three times in Psa 136:8., corresponds to the time of the composition of the Psalm which is required by its contents. It is just the same with the paragogic <hi type="italic">i</hi> in the future in Psa 136:6. But in other respects the language is classic; and the rhythm, at the beginning softly elegiac, then more and more excited, and abounding in guttural and sibilant sounds, is so expressive that scarcely any Psalm is so easily impressed on the memory as this, which is so pictorial even in sound. <div eID="gen10259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10260" type="x-p"/> The metre resembles the elegiac as it appears in the so-called caesura schema of the Lamentations and in the cadence of <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9-Isa.16.10">Isa 16:9-10</reference>, which is like the Sapphic strophe. Every second lien corresponds to the pentameter of the elegiac metre.
entries.0b5cff7b36576e747aa0e9a5b20a22e58dcea9ea: <reference osisRef="Ps.137.1-Ps.137.6">Psa 137:1-6</reference> <div eID="gen10260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10261" type="x-p"/> Beginning with perfects, the Psalm has the appearance of being a Psalm not belonging to the Exile, but written in memory of the Exile. The bank of a river, like the seashore, is a favourite place of sojourn of those whom deep grief drives forth from the bustle of men into solitude. The boundary line of the river gives to solitude a safe back; the monotonous splashing of the waves keeps up the dull, melancholy alternation of thoughts and feelings; and at the same time the sight of the cool, fresh water exercises a soothing influence upon the consuming fever within the heart. The rivers of Babylon are here those of the Babylonian empire: not merely the Euphrates with its canals, and the Tigris, but also the Chaboras (<hi type="italic">Chebar</hi>) and Eulaeos (<hi type="italic">'Ulai</hi>), on whose lonesome banks Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.1.3">Eze 1:3</reference>) and Daniel (ch. <reference osisRef="Dan.8.2">Dan 8:2</reference>) beheld divine visions. The שׁם is important: there, in a strange land, as captives under the dominion of the power of the world. And גּם is purposely chosen instead of ו: with the sitting down in the solitude of the river’s banks weeping immediately came on; when the natural scenery around contrasted so strongly with that of their native land, the remembrance of Zion only forced itself upon them all the more powerfully, and the pain at the isolation from their home would have all the freer course where no hostilely observant eyes were present to suppress it. The willow (צפצפה) and viburnum, those trees which are associated with flowing water in hot low-lying districts, are indigenous in the richly watered lowlands of Babylonia. ערב (ערבה), if one and the same with Arab. <hi type="italic">grb</hi>, is not the willow, least of all the weeping-willow, which is called <hi type="italic">ṣafsâf mustahı̂</hi> in Arabic, “the bending-down willow,” but the viburnum with dentate leaves, described by Wetzstein on Isa 44:4. The Talmud even distinguishes between <hi type="italic">tsaph - tsapha</hi> and <hi type="italic">‛araba</hi>, but without our being able to obtain any sure botanic picture from it. The ערבה, whose branches belong to the constituents of the <hi type="italic">lulab</hi> of the Feast of Tabernacles (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev 23:40</reference>), is understood of the crack-willow [<hi type="italic">Salix fragilis</hi>], and even in the passage before us is surely not distinguished with such botanical precision but that the <hi type="italic">gharab</hi> and willow together with the weeping-willow (<hi type="italic">Salix Babylonica</hi>) might be comprehended under the word ערבה. On these trees of the country abounding in streams the exiles hung their citherns. The time to take delight in music was past, for μουσικὰ ἐν πένθει ἄκαιρος διήγησις, Sir. 22:6. Joyous songs, as the word שׁיר designates them, were ill suited to their situation. <div eID="gen10261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10262" type="x-p"/> In order to understand the כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">Psa 137:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">Psa 137:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.137.4">Psa 137:4</reference> must be taken together. They hung up their citherns; for though their lords called upon them to sing in order that they might divert themselves with their national songs, they did not feel themselves in the mind for singing songs as they once resounded at the divine services of their native land. The lxx, Targum, and Syriac take תּוללינוּ as a synonym of שׁובינוּ, synonymous with שׁוללינוּ, and so, in fact, that it signifies not, like שׁולל, the spoiled and captive one, but the spoiler and he who takes other prisoners. But there is no Aramaic תּלל = שׁלל. It might more readily be referred back to a <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> תּולל (= התל), to disappoint, deride (Hitzig); but the usage of the language does not favour this, and a stronger meaning for the word would be welcome. Either תּולל = תּהולל, like מהולל, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.9">Psa 102:9</reference>, signifies the raving one, i.e., a bloodthirsty man or a tyrant, or from ילל, <hi type="italic">ejulare</hi>, one who causes the cry of woe or a tormentor, - a signification which commends itself in view of the words תּושׁב and תּלמיד, which are likewise formed with the preformative ת. According to the sense the word ranks itself with an <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הוליל, like תּועלת, תּוכחה, with הועיל and הוכיח, in a mainly abstract signification (Dietrich, <hi type="italic">Abhandlungen</hi>, S. 160f.). The דּברי beside שׁיר is used as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.20">Psa 35:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Psa 65:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.27">Psa 105:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">Psa 145:5</reference>, viz., partitively, dividing up the genitival notion of the species: words of songs as being parts or fragments of the national treasury of song, similar to משּׁיר a little further on, on which Rosenmüller correctly says: <hi type="italic">sacrum aliquod carmen ex veteribus illis suis Sionicis</hi>. With the expression “song of Zion” alternates in <reference osisRef="Ps.137.4">Psa 137:4</reference> “song of Jahve,” which, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.27">2Ch 29:27</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.7">1Ch 25:7</reference>, denotes sacred or liturgical songs, that is to say, songs belonging to Psalm poesy (including the <hi type="italic">Cantica</hi>). <div eID="gen10262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10263" type="x-p"/> Before <reference osisRef="Ps.137.4">Psa 137:4</reference> we have to imagine that they answered the request of the Babylonians at that time in the language that follows, or thought thus within themselves when they withdrew themselves from them. The meaning of the interrogatory exclamation is not that the singing of sacred songs in a foreign land (חוצה לארץ) is contrary to the law, for the Psalms continued to be sung even during the Exile, and were also enriched by new ones. But the <hi type="italic">shir</hi> had an end during the Exile, in so far as that it was obliged to retire from publicity into the quiet of the family worship and of the houses of prayer, in order that that which is holy might not be profaned; and since it was not, as at home, accompanied by the trumpets of the priests and the music of the Levites, it became more recitative than singing properly so called, and therefore could not afford any idea of the singing of their native land in connection with the worship of God on Zion. From the striking contrast between the present and the former times the people of the Exile had in fact to come to the knowledge of their sins, in order that they might get back by the way of penitence and earnest longing to that which they had lost Penitence and home-sickness were at that time inseparable; for all those in whom the remembrance of Zion was lost gave themselves over to heathenism and were excluded from the redemption. The poet, translated into the situation of the exiles, and arming himself against the temptation to apostasy and the danger of denying God, therefore says: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, ימיני תּשׁכּח. תּשׁכּח has been taken as an address to Jahve: <hi type="italic">obliviscaris dexterae meae</hi> (e.g., Wolfgang Dachstein in his song “<hi type="italic">An Wasserflüssen Babylon</hi>”), but it is far from natural that Jerusalem and Jahve should be addressed in one clause. Others take ימיני as the subject and תּשׁכּח transitively: <hi type="italic">obliviscatur dextera mea, scil. artem psallendi</hi> (Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Pagninus, Grotius, Hengstenberg, and others); but this ellipsis is arbitrary, and the interpolation of מנּי after ימיני (von Ortenberg, following Olshausen) produces an inelegant cadence. Others again assign a passive sense to תשׁכח: <hi type="italic">oblivioni detur</hi> (lxx, Italic, Vulgate, and Luther), or a half-passive sense, <hi type="italic">in oblivione sit</hi> (Jerome); but the thought: let my right hand be forgotten, is awkward and tame. <hi type="italic">Obliviscatur me</hi> (Syriac, Saadia, and the Psalterium Romanum) comes nearer to the true meaning. תּשׁכּח is to be taken reflexively: <hi type="italic">obliviscatur sui ipsius</hi>, let it forget itself, or its service (Amyraldus, Schultens, Ewald, and Hitzig), which is equivalent to let it refuse or fail, become lame, become benumbed, much the same as we say of the arms of legs that they “go to sleep,” and just as the Arabic <hi type="italic">nasiya</hi> signifies both to forget and to become lame (cf. Gesenius, <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>, p. 921 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). La Harpe correctly renders: <hi type="italic">O Jerusalem! si je t'oublie jamais, que ma main oublie aussi le mouvement!</hi> Thus there is a correspondence between <reference osisRef="Ps.137.5">Psa 137:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.137.6">Psa 137:6</reference> : My tongue shall cleave to my palate if I do not remember thee, if I do not raise Jerusalem above the sum of my joy. אזכּרכי has the affixed <hi type="italic">Chirek</hi>, with which these later Psalms are so fond of adorning themselves. ראשׁ is apparently used as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.160">Psa 119:160</reference> : <hi type="italic">supra summam</hi> (the totality) <hi type="italic">laetitiae meae</hi>, as Coccejus explains, <hi type="italic">h.e. supra omnem laetitiam meam</hi>. But why not then more simply על כּל, above the totality? ראשׁ here signifies not κεφάλαιον, but κεφαλή: if I do not place Jerusalem upon the summit of my joy, i.e., my highest joy; therefore, if I do not cause Jerusalem to be my very highest joy. His spiritual joy over the city of God is to soar above all earthly joys.
entries.61e43e3db8dbec18f85f41b08309ae73cdc5d678: <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7-Ps.137.9">Psa 137:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen10263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10264" type="x-p"/> The second part of the Psalm supplicates vengeance upon Edom and Babylon. We see from Obadiah’s prophecy, which is taken up again by Jeremiah, how shamefully the Edomites, that brother-people related by descent to Israel and yet pre-eminently hostile to it, behaved in connection with the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldaeans as their malignant, rapacious, and inhuman helpers. The repeated <hi type="italic">imper. Piel</hi> ערוּ, from ערה (not <hi type="italic">imper. Kal</hi> from ערר, which would be ערוּ), ought to have been accented on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>.; it is, however, in both cases accented on the first syllable, the pausal ערוּ (cf. כּלוּ in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>, and also הסּוּ, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.11">Neh 8:11</reference>) giving rise to the same accentuation of the other (in order that two tone-syllables might not come together). The <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> also stands between the two repeated words in order that they may be duly separated, and secures, moreover, to the guttural initial of the second ערוּ its distinct pronunciation (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.26.28">Gen 26:28</reference>; Num 35:16). It is to be construed: lay bare, lay bare (as in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.13">Hab 3:13</reference>, cf. גּלּה in Mic 1:6) in it (<hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the place), of in respect of it (<hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the object), even to the foundation, i.e., raze it even to the ground, leave not one stone upon another. From the false brethren the imprecation turns to Babylon, the city of the imperial power of the world. The daughter, i.e., the population, of Babylon is addressed as השּׁדוּדה. It certainly seems the most natural to take this epithet as a designation of its doings which cry for vengeance. But it cannot in any case be translated: thou plunderer (Syriac like the Targum: <hi type="italic">bozuzto</hi>; Symmachus ἡ λῃστρίς), for שׁדד does not mean to rob and plunder, but to offer violence and to devastate. Therefore: thou devastator; but the word so pointed as we have it before us cannot have this signification: it ought to be השּׁדודה, like בּגודה in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.7">Jer 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.10">Jer 3:10</reference>, or השּׁדוּדה (with an unchangeable <hi type="italic">ā</hi>), corresponding to the Syriac active intensive form <hi type="italic">ālûṣo</hi>, oppressor, <hi type="italic">gōdûfo</hi>, slanderer, and the Arabic likewise active intensive form Arab. <hi type="italic">fâ‛ûl</hi>, e.g., <hi type="italic">fâshûs</hi>, a boaster, and also as an adjective: <hi type="italic">ǵôz fâshûs</hi>, empty nuts, cf. יקוּשׁ = יקושׁ, a fowler, like <hi type="italic">nâṭûr</hi> (נאטור), a field-watcher. The form as it stands is <hi type="italic">part. pass.</hi>, and signifies προνενομευμένη (Aquila), <hi type="italic">vastata</hi> (Jerome). It is possible that this may be said in the sense of <hi type="italic">vastanda</hi>, although in this sense of a <hi type="italic">part. fut. pass</hi>. the participles of the <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> (e.g., Ps 22:32; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.19">Psa 102:19</reference>) and of the <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference>) are more commonly used. It cannot at any rate signify <hi type="italic">vastata</hi> in an historical sense, with reference to the destruction of Babylon by Darius Hystaspes (Hengstenberg); for <reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference> only prays that the retribution may come: it cannot therefore as yet have been executed; but if השׁדודה signified the already devastated one, it must (at least in the main) have been executed already. It might be more readily understood as a prophetical representation of the executed judgment of devastation; but this prophetic rendering coincides with the imprecative: the imagination of the Semite when he utters a curse sees the future as a realized fact. “Didst thou see the smitten one (<hi type="italic">maḍrûb</hi>),” i.e., he whom God must smite? Thus the Arab inquires for a person who is detested. “Pursue him who is seized (<hi type="italic">ilḥaḳ el̇ma'chûdh</hi>),” i.e., him whom God must allow thee to seize! Thy speak thus inasmuch as the imagination at once anticipates the seizure at the same time with the pursuit. Just as here both <hi type="italic">maḍrûb</hi> and <hi type="italic">ma'chûdh</hi> are participles of <hi type="italic">Kasl</hi>, so therefore השּׁדוּודה may also have the sense of <hi type="italic">vastanda</hi> (which must be laid waste!). That which is then further desired for Babylon is the requital of that which it has done to Israel, Isa 47:6. It is the same penal destiny, comprehending the children also, which is predicted against it in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.16-Isa.13.18">Isa 13:16-18</reference>, as that which was to be executed by the Medes. The young children (with reference to עולל, עולל, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.8.3">Psa 8:3</reference>) are to be dashed to pieces in order that a new generation may not raise up again the world-wide dominion that has been overthrown, Isa 14:21. It is zeal for God that puts such harsh words into the mouth of the poet. “That which is Israel’s excellency and special good fortune the believing Israelite desires to have bestowed upon the whole world, but for this very reason he desires to see the hostility of the present world of nations against the church of God broken” (Hofmann). On the other hand, it cannot be denied that the “blessed” of this Psalm is not suited to the mouth of the New Testament church. In the Old Testament the church as yet had the form of a nation, and the longing for the revelation of divine righteousness clothed itself accordingly in a warlike garb.  <chapter eID="Ps.137"/> <div eID="gen10264" type="x-p"/>

entries.5d8f7ab37e91d2f605e11a2152726c9c0583d2e2:
PSALM 137
At the Babylonish captivity the established order of God’s worship was overthrown, and the Psalmist complains, in the name of the Church at large, of the taunts which the enemy east upon the name of God, addressing at the same time a word of comfort to his people under their captivity, to cheer them with the hope of deliverance.
Psalm 137:1-4
1. By the rivers of Babylon there we sat down, we even wept when we remembered thee, O Zion! 2. We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof. 3. Then they that carried us away captive required of us the words of a song, and mirth when we were in suspense, saying, Sing to us one of the songs of Zion. 4. How shall we sing Jehovah’s song in a foreign land?
 
1. By the rivers of Babylon
By “Babylon” is meant, not the city, but the kingdom; and the mention of rivers, according to the suggestion of Rosenmuller, is because the synagogues were usually built near rivers, for the greater convenience of the Jews, who were obliged to wash their hands before prayer. But as they had no synagogues in Babylon, they might frequent such localities as would, be suitable sites for places of worship, and there in the open air perform divine service. It is conjectured by Chrysostom that the Jewish captives were not suffered at first to dwell in any of their conquerors’ towns or cities, but were dispersed all along several rivers of the country, where they built for themselves tabernacles or cottages.
there we sat down I have elsewhere said, that it is a great mistake to suppose that it is David who here prophetically apprises the people of God of the captivity which should come upon them. The Prophets in speaking of future events employ very different language. What is brought under notice is the event as now historically come, and matter of experience. We shall briefly explain the scope of the Psalmist. There was danger that the Jews when cast off in such a melancholy manner should lose hold altogether of their faith and of their religion. Considering how ready we are, when mixed up with the wicked and ungodly, to fall into superstition or evil practices, it was to be feared that they might wax profane amongst the population of Babylon. The people of the Lord might be thrown into despondency, besides, by their captivity, the cruel bondage they were subjected to, and the other indignities which they had to endure. The writer of this Psalm, whose name is unknown, drew up a form of lamentation, that by giving expression to their sufferings in sighs and prayers, they might keep alive the hope of that deliverance which they despaired of. Another end he has in view, is to warn them against, the decline of godliness in an irreligious land, and against; defilement with the contaminations of the heathen. Accordingly he denounces merited judgment upon the children of Edom, and declares that Babylon, whose prosperity, shortlived as it was destined to be in itself, eclipsed at that time the rest of the world, was an object of pity, and near to destruction. The length of time during which the captivity lasted, may of itself convince us how useful and even necessary it must have been to support the fainting minds of God’s people. They must have been ready to acquiesce in the corrupt practices of the heathen, unless endued with surprising mental fortitude through a period of seventy years.
When they are said to have sat, this denotes a continued period of captivity, that they were not only torn from the sight of their native country, but in a manner buried and entombed.
It may also be observed that sitting on the ground is a posture which indicates mourning and deep distress. Thus it is said in Isaiah 3:26, where the captivity of the Jews in Babylon is foretold, “And she [Judea] being desolate shall sit upon the ground.” And the Prophet Jeremiah, in portraying the sorrow which afflicted his pious and patriotic countrymen under the desolation of their country, says,
“The elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground and keep silence.” (Lamentations 2:10 )
“We find Judea,” says Mr. Addison, “on several coins of Vespasian and Titus in a posture that denotes sorrow and captivity. I need not mention her sitting on the ground, because we have already spoken of the aptness of such a posture to represent an extreme affliction. I fancy the Romans might have an eye on the customs of the Jewish nation, as well as those of their own country, in the several marks of sorrow they have set on this figure. The Psalmist describes the Jews lamenting their captivity in the same pensive posture: ‘By the waters of Babylon we sat down and wept, when we remembered thee, O Zion!’” — Addison on Medals, Dial. 2.
The demonstrative adverb of place, שם, sham, there, is emphatical, setting the subject, as it were, before the eyes of the reader. Though the pleasantness of the country, irrigated by streams, might have had an effect in soothing their dejected minds, we are told that the Lord’s people, so long as they dwelt there, were continually in tears. The particle גם, gam, even, is used as being intensative, to let us know that the true fearers of the Lord could not be tempted by all the luxuries of Babylon to forget their native inheritance. The language is such as to intimate at the same time that they were not so entirely overwhelmed by their calamities as not to recognize in them the deserved chatisement of God, and that they were not chargeable with obstinately struggling against him; for tears are the expression of humility and penitence, as well as of distress. This appears still more plainly from its being Zion they remembered, which proves that what had charms for them was not any advantage of a worldly kind they might there enjoy:, but the worship of God. God had erected his sanctuary like a flag upon mount Zion, that as often as they looked to it, they might be assured of his salvation. Fair then and fertile as was the region where they dwelt, with charms which could corrupt effeminate minds, and long as they ‘were detained in it, tears, which are proverbially soon dried up, never ceased to stream from their eyes, because they were cut off from the worship of God, upon which they ‘were wont to attend, and felt that they were torn from the inheritance of promise.
